participants: Chris Klevan (Primal Instinct) — sales lead/manager, runs the meeting
Adam A. (Primal Instinct) — setter/closer in training
Referenced but not present: Trevor (founder/coach), Caden (head coach), Andrew (closer, Poland), Angelo (ops)
summary: End-of-month sales team meeting followed by a group call-review training. The first eleven minutes are a wins round and a cash-collection check against monthly projections, with the manager confirming the team has hit its targets and pushing individual reps toward their bonus thresholds. The remaining forty-eight minutes are a line-by-line group review of a recorded closing call Chris Klevan ran with a prospect who goes by the nickname 'Myth' — a trader who plays padel daily, has trained with kettlebells for four years, and had gone inconsistent. Chris pauses the recording repeatedly to explain his reasoning and takes questions from Adam, Derek, Kim and Richard on framing, pre-handling objections, when to run consequence, and how much to say versus draw out of the prospect. The reviewed call ends with the prospect closed on a $1,200 thirty-day 'love it or leave it' trial after stating three separate times that he was not ready to decide.
notable: SETTER CODE MAPPING RESOLVED. The three setter initials used across the corpus are all present in this meeting: Kim Forbes-Sobers (KFS), Derek Harris (DH — previously recorded as unknown), and a fourth team member, Adam A. This confirms the 'Derek' referenced in the 07/30 Michael Hogan call.

THE 'LOVE IT OR LEAVE IT' PRICE IS $1,200. Chris Klevan states it on the reviewed call: 'the actual price of the program is $6,000... We have what's called a love it or leave it... It would be $1,200. You would commit to 30 days.' Continuation is 'you can pay the remaining $4,800.' This is the same structure Richard Claessen improvised with Marcus Mahar on 07/29 where the amount was never spoken aloud — this meeting supplies the missing figure and shows the structure is a sanctioned, manager-taught play rather than a one-off improvisation.

A PERFORMANCE GUARANTEE EXISTS AND IS DEPLOYED OPPORTUNISTICALLY. On the reviewed call: 'if you don't get to a point where you've put on 16kg of strength on your kettlebell lifts, then we will literally keep working with you for free until you do.' In the debrief Chris confirms it was unplanned — 'I honestly just realized that this guy needed more certainty, so I threw the guarantee' — and when Richard notes 'you don't always want to hang on a guarantee', Chris answers 'If you have it, use it. Why not? What is it going to hurt?' No guarantee was mentioned on any of the nine sales calls in this batch.

A DELIBERATE IDENTITY-OBSCURING PHONE TECHNIQUE IS SHARED AND ADOPTED. Derek Harris teaches the team to defeat AI call screeners by giving only a first name and going silent so the prospect believes they already know the caller: 'they pick up at a so much higher rate because they think that they know you.' Kim Forbes-Sobers says she will use it. The manager responds 'All right, let's go. Helping the team out.'

CONSUMER CREDIT FINANCED A CLOSE AND WAS CELEBRATED. 'You found another $5,000 and got that guy on Klarna, dude. Like, absolutely fantastic.' Richard clarifies he did not arrange it — 'I guess you sent him the payment link and he just Klarna'd it himself' — but the buy-now-pay-later close was praised as the reason monthly projections were hit.

THE TEAM SEES AND DISCUSSES PROSPECTS' CREDIT SCORES AND INCOME. Two prospects are discussed by 'financial grade' ('a 3.53 financial grade', 'he had a 3.25 FG'), and Kim comments on data reliability: 'I think the credit score is pretty accurate, but the actual income on the sales kick can be a little bit off.'

RICHARD LEARNED THE UPGRADE-CREDIT POLICY IN THIS MEETING AND FRAMED IT AS AN UPSELL LEVER: 'now that I do know that we put the thousands, or however much he spent, also towards the one-on-one. And that will definitely help with upselling people.' He had already promised that credit to prospects on 07/29 and 07/30, and contradicted himself about it three times on the 07/31 Rohan Bhatnagar call.

RICHARD CONFIRMS A DELIBERATE TWO-TIER PRESENTATION STRATEGY as a personal win: 'I did pitch, like, the two offers at the same time... instead of having to go through that sort of down-selling him and making it seem like a second-choice option.' This is the pattern visible across four of his calls in this batch.

MONTH-END BONUS PRESSURE IS EXPLICIT. 'You need about 11k to hit your projections to get your bonus, 11k, don't count it out bro, you've got four calls... 12k is absolutely in sight, you could get two piffs, and then boom, you're right at projections.' The meeting frames the remaining days as 'just racking it up and just finishing up, getting as much cash as we can.'

A CLOSING CALL STOPPED RECORDING MID-CLOSE. 'That's why it stopped recording, because I had to call Andrew real quick.' The manager had assumed from the recording that the deal was lost until told otherwise. Recordings in this corpus are not a complete record of closes.
CLIENT VOLUME CLAIM: on the reviewed call Chris tells the prospect 'we work with 1,200 guys, and a lot of business owners'. Worth reconciling against actual active client count.

PRODUCT NAME CONFIRMED: 'Primal University' is the entry tier; Kim discusses a University client, Adonay, by name and progress, and Chris asks 'we got to get him up to Kettlebell Body, what are we going to do?' Richard says he closed Adonay roughly two weeks earlier and plans to upsell him.

COACHING PHILOSOPHY ON PRESSURE. Chris teaches asking permission to be blunt as an access device: 'If you get permission to be totally blunt with somebody, you could pretty much say almost anything to them, and it's like, dude, you said I have permission.' He also describes the close as 'I kind of big-brothered him' and 'I needed him to take a line of credit out on my certainty.'

CONSEQUENCE PHASE IS ADMITTEDLY NOT RUN BY THE SALES LEAD. 'To be honest, I don't do a lot of consequence. I don't do a lot of consequence questions. Personally, just never, never did.' Adam pushes back that leverage was missed. This is relevant to interpreting P5 adherence across the whole corpus — the phase is weakly modelled from the top.

One genuinely positive note worth recording: the team explicitly coaches against overpromising. Chris declines to promise a fighter physique in six months, and Richard reinforces it — 'when someone is already lean and you tell them yeah, we can easily get you in fighter shape... you're just selling them a line. They feel that as well.' Chris: 'Always tell the truth. Be honest.'
